objectives: Distinguish X-ray/CT, MRI, ultrasound, PET physics.
Reason about contrast + dose + resolution tradeoffs.
Connect modality choice to clinical questions.

slides.title: X-ray, CT, MRI, ultrasound, PET: fundamentals
slides.body:
**X-ray** (Röntgen 1895): photons (~30-150 keV) attenuated by tissue. Bone absorbs more (high-Z Ca); air least. 2D projection. Dose: ~0.1 mSv chest X-ray. Cheap, fast, widely available. Limited soft-tissue contrast.

**CT (computed tomography)**: rotating X-ray source + detectors; 3D reconstruction via Radon transform (Hounsfield 1972). Sub-mm resolution. Dose: 5-10 mSv abdomen-pelvis CT (~3 yr background equivalent). Excellent for trauma (bleeding, fractures), lung (nodules), abdominal pathology. CT angiography for coronary + vascular.

**MRI (magnetic resonance imaging)**: strong magnetic field (1.5T, 3T, 7T+) + RF pulses excite ¹H nuclei in water; precessional signal decay (T1 + T2) reconstructed via Fourier inversion in k-space. No ionizing radiation. Excellent soft-tissue contrast. Slow (~30-60 min). Expensive. Contraindications: pacemakers (newer ones MR-conditional), metal implants. Functional MRI (fMRI) for brain mapping via BOLD signal.

**Ultrasound**: high-frequency sound waves (~2-15 MHz) reflected from tissue interfaces. Echo timing + intensity → image. Real-time. Cheap. No radiation. Operator-dependent. Limited by gas (can't image lung) + bone (acoustic-shadow). Doppler ultrasound measures blood velocity. Echocardiography for cardiac structure + function.

**PET (positron emission tomography)**: radiolabeled tracer (¹⁸F-FDG glucose analog most common; T½ = 110 min) administered IV. β⁺ decay + annihilation produces back-to-back 511-keV photons; coincidence-detection 3D image. Functional imaging — metabolism, receptors. Oncology (tumor detection + staging), neurology (Alzheimer's). High dose (~7 mSv FDG-PET) + expensive. Combined PET-CT or PET-MRI for anatomical + functional fusion.

slides.title: Resolution + contrast + SNR tradeoffs
slides.body:
Image quality dimensions:
• **Spatial resolution**: smallest distinguishable feature. CT ~0.5 mm; MRI ~1 mm clinical (sub-mm research); ultrasound ~0.1-1 mm (frequency-dependent); PET ~3-5 mm.
• **Temporal resolution**: how fast images acquired. Ultrasound 30+ fps; fMRI ~1-2 sec/volume; MRI minutes/volume traditionally.
• **Contrast resolution**: ability to distinguish similar tissues. MRI > CT > ultrasound for soft-tissue contrast.
• **SNR (signal-to-noise ratio)**: contrast / standard deviation of noise. Higher SNR = clearer image.
• **Dose** (ionizing modalities): mSv equivalent. ALARA principle.

**Tradeoffs are fundamental**:
- Higher resolution → smaller voxels → fewer signal photons → lower SNR. To maintain SNR, increase dose or scan time.
- Faster scan → less averaging → lower SNR.
- Larger field of view → coarser resolution at fixed pixel count.

**MRI k-space + contrast**: image acquired in spatial-frequency (k-space) domain via gradient encoding. Center of k-space = low frequencies = contrast; edges = high frequencies = detail. Partial k-space sampling (parallel imaging GRAPPA, SENSE; compressed sensing) accelerates by 2-8×.

**Deep learning in imaging**:
- Reconstruction: AUTOMAP, MoDL, Variational Networks for accelerated MRI.
- Segmentation: nnU-Net + variants for tissue + tumor.
- Detection: chest X-ray pneumonia, CT lung nodule, mammography mass.
- Multi-modal fusion: PET-CT joint analysis.
- FDA SaMD pathway: ~600+ AI/ML medical devices cleared by 2024.

slides.title: Modality selection + clinical scenarios
slides.body:
**Clinical questions drive modality choice**:
• **Trauma + acute bleeding**: CT (whole-body trauma CT; angio for vascular).
• **Fractures**: X-ray first; CT for complex; MRI for stress fractures + soft-tissue injury.
• **Stroke**:
  - Acute (<4.5 hr from onset): non-contrast CT to exclude bleeding before thrombolytics.
  - CT perfusion / CT angiography or MRI for penumbra + occluded vessel; informs mechanical thrombectomy decision (within 6-24 hr).
• **MI (cardiac)**: ECG + troponin; echocardiogram for function; coronary CT angiography (CCTA) for anatomy; SPECT/PET for myocardial perfusion.
• **Lung pathology**: chest X-ray (TB, pneumonia screening); CT for nodule (lung cancer screening LDCT every 1-2 yr in high-risk).
• **Abdominal pain**: ultrasound first (gallbladder, kidney, appendix in children); CT if uncertain.
• **Cancer staging**: CT + PET-CT for most solid tumors; MRI for liver, brain, prostate, soft tissue.
• **Brain**:
  - CT for trauma + hemorrhage + bone.
  - MRI for stroke, tumor, MS, dementia, epilepsy.
  - fMRI for surgical planning + research.
• **Joint + spine**: MRI for ligament, disc, cartilage, marrow.
• **Obstetrics**: ultrasound mainstay; MRI for fetal anatomy in select cases.

**Cost + access**:
- X-ray: ~$50-200; ubiquitous.
- CT: ~$300-1000; widely available.
- MRI: ~$500-2500; common in hospitals.
- PET-CT: ~$2000-5000; tertiary centers.
- Ultrasound: ~$100-500; portable + bedside.

**Equity**: imaging access varies vastly globally. Many LMICs lack MRI/PET. AI + portable ultrasound (Butterfly iQ, GE Vscan) increasing access.

**Radiation dose stewardship**: cumulative dose tracking; pediatric protocols (lower dose); avoid unnecessary CTs (lifetime cancer risk from medical radiation: ~1.5-2% of US cancer in 2020 attributed).

question.question: Pick the right imaging modality for each scenario
question.goal: Match clinical scenario to optimal imaging modality.

steps.prompt: 60-yo with sudden-onset hemiparesis. Time = 90 min from onset. First imaging?
hints: Need to exclude hemorrhage before thrombolytics.
steps.reveal: **Non-contrast CT head** — must exclude hemorrhagic stroke before considering tPA. Sensitive to acute bleed; less so to early ischemia (may look normal early in ischemic stroke, but exclusion of bleed is the priority within 4.5 hr window). Then CT angiography + perfusion or MRI DWI/PWI to characterize ischemic core + penumbra; informs mechanical thrombectomy decision (window 6-24 hr if mismatch favorable).

steps.prompt: Pregnant patient with right-lower-quadrant pain, suspected appendicitis. Imaging?
steps.reveal: **Ultrasound** is first-line for suspected appendicitis in pregnancy — no ionizing radiation, sensitive when appendix visualized. If non-diagnostic: **MRI without contrast** (gadolinium contraindicated in pregnancy) is next step. CT only as last resort with informed consent for radiation risk.

steps.prompt: 70-yo with chronic back pain + suspected vertebral compression fracture. Imaging?

acceptedAnswers: MRI to differentiate acute from chronic + tumor

steps.reveal: **X-ray initially** to confirm fracture; **MRI** to distinguish acute from chronic (acute fractures show marrow edema = high T2 / STIR signal) + to exclude tumor (metastases — pathological fractures common in elderly + cancer patients). Decision affects treatment: kyphoplasty for acute; biopsy + oncology workup for malignant cause.

steps.prompt: Patient with newly-diagnosed lung adenocarcinoma. Staging?
steps.reveal: **FDG PET-CT** — combined whole-body PET (functional, FDG uptake correlates with tumor metabolism) + CT (anatomical). Stages primary tumor (T), regional + distant nodes (N), metastases (M). Particularly good for distant metastases (bone, adrenal, contralateral lung) that change treatment. Brain MRI added for adenocarcinoma (frequent brain mets). Modern lung-cancer staging: PET-CT + brain MRI + EBUS-TBNA biopsy of suspicious nodes.

question.question: Drag the slider to estimate the radiation dose (in mSv) of a typical abdomen-pelvis CT scan.
question.explanation: Abdomen-pelvis CT: ~8-10 mSv (varies with technique + body size). For comparison: background ~3 mSv/yr; chest X-ray ~0.1 mSv; mammogram ~0.4 mSv; head CT ~2 mSv; PET-CT ~7 mSv; nuclear cardiac stress ~10-15 mSv. Cumulative dose from multiple imaging is a growing concern; ALARA principle + appropriate-use criteria + low-dose protocols (iterative reconstruction) reduce.

question.question: Classify each imaging finding by the modality that best demonstrates it.
question.explanation:
Each modality has clinical strengths:
• **Plain X-ray**: bony structures, gross thoracic + abdominal pathology, post-procedure check. Cheap, fast.
• **CT**: detailed cross-section; bone, lung, abdomen, vascular, trauma, acute hemorrhage. Higher dose.
• **MRI**: soft tissue, brain, spine, joints, MS, prostate, breast (problem cases), fetal anatomy. No radiation; slow + contraindicated for some implants.
• **Ultrasound**: heart + abdomen + obstetrics + vascular (DVT, carotid) + pregnancy + bedside (FAST exam, lung sliding). Real-time; cheap; no radiation; operator-dependent.
• **PET**: functional/metabolic; oncology staging + restaging; neurology (dementia); cardiac viability. Combined PET-CT or PET-MRI for fusion.

Clinical decision-making integrates: question being asked, prior probability of disease, urgency, cost + access, contraindications, patient preference. Multiple imaging studies are often needed; complementary information matters.

question.question: If an MRI scanner has B₀ = 3 T, what's the ¹H Larmor frequency (in MHz)? Use γ/2π = 42.58 MHz/T.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain why MRI gives much better soft-tissue contrast than CT, even though both produce 3D images.
question.rubric: Mentions: CT contrast based on electron density (X-ray attenuation): bone > soft tissue > air. Soft tissues all similar density → poor differentiation. MRI contrast based on tissue water content + relaxation times (T1, T2) + chemical environment. T1: longitudinal relaxation; T2: transverse. Sequences (T1w, T2w, FLAIR, DWI, susceptibility-weighted) emphasize different mechanisms. Result: muscle/fat/bone/CSF/gray/white matter all have distinct signal intensities. Pathology (edema, tumor, demyelination, hemorrhage) modifies T1/T2 → clear visualization. CT advantages: faster, less expensive, fewer contraindications, better for bone + acute bleed + lung. Choice depends on question: 'is there bleeding?' → CT; 'what's the soft-tissue lesion?' → MRI; both for complex problems. Modern hybrid PET-MRI captures functional + structural information together.
